'''Nikola Tesla''' (1856–1943) was a Serbian-American electrical engineer whose polyphase alternating-current system is the one the world actually runs on. He is also the figure around whom the largest volume of invented history in the history of technology has accumulated — which is a reason to be careful with him, not a reason to avoid him. The patents are public documents, and they are more interesting than the folklore.

== Why he matters to this Institute ==

Two threads. First, the '''resonance and frequency''' work: Tesla's whole programme after 1890 was the transmission of energy through resonant coupling — tuned circuits, standing waves, and the earth itself treated as a resonant cavity. The entrainment material in this library is a much smaller claim of the same shape: that a system with a natural frequency can be driven at that frequency. Second, '''wireless transmission through a natural medium''' is the direct ancestor of every argument about fields and bodies that the neurostimulation literature now has to make carefully.

He is not evidence for anything in the [[Stack Substances|pharmacology]]. He is a lineage, and this page keeps the two apart.

== The patent list ==

Tesla held roughly 300 patents across 26 countries. These are the ones worth knowing, with what each actually claims. '''Verify any number against USPTO or Google Patents before formal citation''' — this list is a reading guide, not a certified docket.

== Vivekananda, Akasha and Prana ==

Tesla met [[Swami Vivekananda]] in New York in early 1896. Vivekananda's letter of 13 February 1896
records Tesla's belief that he could "demonstrate mathematically that force and matter are reducible
to potential energy," and Vivekananda's hope that this would place Vedantic cosmology "on the surest
of foundations."

'''Tesla never produced the demonstration.''' No paper, no derivation, no follow-up. The popular
retelling of this meeting almost always stops at the letter, one paragraph before the disappointment.

What Tesla did do is better attested. In "Man's Greatest Achievement" — drafted 1907, published in the
''New York American'' in 1930 — he wrote:

: "All perceptible matter comes from a primary substance, or tenuity beyond conception, filling all
space, the ''Akasha'' or luminiferous ether, which is acted upon by the life-giving ''Prana'' or
creative force, calling into existence, in never-ending cycles, all things and phenomena."

A real transmission, from a Bengali monk into the published prose of the man who built the AC grid —
and, at the same time, a restatement of '''luminiferous aether''', a hypothesis already in trouble in
1907 and since abandoned. The Sanskrit did not save it. See
[[Mysticism and Eastern Philosophy in Science]].

== What is true, and what is not ==

'''True and under-appreciated:''' the induction motor and polyphase system are the foundation of industrial electrification. The radio-controlled boat of 1898 is a real and startling artefact. The Tesla valve is a working fluidic diode still being studied. The Supreme Court's 1943 decision in ''Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. v. United States'' upheld Tesla's priority on several radio claims — often overstated as "Tesla invented radio," which is not what the ruling says, but the priority finding is real.

'''Not established:''' the earthquake machine as usually told; the death ray; wireless power at Wardenclyffe scale, which was never demonstrated and which the physics of ground conduction does not obviously support; and the large body of documents attributed to him after 1943. The FBI's file on the seizure of his papers has been released and is far less interesting than its reputation.

'''The "3, 6, 9" material''' — the vortex-mathematics claims attached to Tesla across the internet — has
no primary source. It does not appear in his patents, papers, interviews or correspondence, and it
should not be cited to him.

The honest summary: '''the real Tesla is a better story than the legendary one''', and the legend has cost him readers who assume the whole thing is folklore.
